# ALS evidence packet — draft v1

This curated input is not a comprehensive review. Every method receives the same UTF-8 file. Summaries are original paraphrases. Bibliographic metadata and abstracts were checked through the public NCBI ID converter and PubMed EFetch on 2026-10-05. Selected studies predate 2025; this does not remove knowledge already in a model's training. Co-Scientist outputs are not included.

## Research question

Propose one specific, testable hypothesis connecting phosphorylation of a nuclear-pore-complex nucleoporin to ALS-related neuronal dysfunction. Explain the causal chain, distinguish an initiating mechanism from a downstream response, and propose an experimental strategy that discriminates the hypothesis from an alternative. Identify supported premises, speculative bridges, and a falsifying observation. This adapts Co-Scientist Supplementary Note 10; nucleoporin phosphorylation is not supplied as an established ALS cause.

## S1 — TDP-43 and nuclear-pore dysfunction

Chou et al. (2018), *TDP-43 pathology disrupts nuclear pore complexes and nucleocytoplasmic transport in ALS/FTD*. Nature Neuroscience. DOI: `10.1038/s41593-017-0047-3`; PMID: `29311743`; PMCID: `PMC5800968`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29311743/).

Nuclear-pore and transport components were associated with insoluble TDP-43 aggregates. Disease-linked TDP-43 disrupted nucleoporin localization and nuclear transport in experimental cell systems; relevant pore pathology was observed in ALS tissue. This supports examining the connection between TDP-43 pathology and transport disruption. It does not identify a nucleoporin phosphorylation event as the initiating cause or establish the same sequence in every ALS subtype.

## S2 — C9orf72-associated transport defects

Zhang et al. (2015), *The C9orf72 repeat expansion disrupts nucleocytoplasmic transport*. Nature. DOI: `10.1038/nature14973`; PMID: `26308891`; PMCID: `PMC4800742`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26308891/).

Expanded C9orf72 repeat RNA was linked to altered RanGAP localization and impaired nuclear import in models and patient-derived neurons. Manipulations of transport or repeat-RNA-associated mechanisms modified model phenotypes. This supplies a genetic-context-specific route to transport dysfunction. It does not show that sporadic ALS arises by the same route or directly establish a nucleoporin phosphorylation mechanism.

## S3 — A stress-granule-independent route

Gasset-Rosa et al. (2019), *Cytoplasmic TDP-43 De-mixing Independent of Stress Granules Drives Inhibition of Nuclear Import, Loss of Nuclear TDP-43, and Cell Death*. Neuron. DOI: `10.1016/j.neuron.2019.02.038`; PMID: `30853299`; PMCID: `PMC6548321`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30853299/).

Persistent cytoplasmic TDP-43 assemblies could form independently of conventional stress granules. They recruited or mislocalized transport-associated proteins and were associated with impaired transport, nuclear TDP-43 depletion, and cell death. Phosphorylated TDP-43 accumulated in these assemblies. That is not itself evidence of nucleoporin phosphorylation. The experimental perturbations do not establish that every physiological ALS trajectory begins in this way.

## S4 — A stress-granule-associated route

Zhang et al. (2018), *Stress Granule Assembly Disrupts Nucleocytoplasmic Transport*. Cell. DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2018.03.025`; PMID: `29628143`; PMCID: `PMC6083872`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29628143/).

Cellular stress recruited transport factors into stress granules and impaired nucleocytoplasmic transport. Altering stress-granule assembly modified transport defects and disease-model phenotypes. This provides a sequestration-based alternative to an intrinsic pore-modification hypothesis. Read alongside S3, it does not justify assuming that conventional stress granules are required for every TDP-43-associated transport defect.

## Evidence boundaries

- These selected passages do not establish that nucleoporin phosphorylation initiates ALS. Label a proposed kinase, modification site, or interaction as an assumption unless a supplied source supports it.
- Specify the ALS context; do not assume a universal mechanism across genetic and sporadic disease.
- Distinguish pore alteration, transport-factor sequestration, and failure secondary to broader stress.
- Explain temporal and perturbational evidence that would distinguish cause from consequence.
- Propose a research hypothesis rather than claiming a mechanism or treatment has been validated.


Proposed answer (the answer to evaluate):
CDK5-dependent NUP98 phosphorylation initiates nuclear-import failure in TARDBP-mutant motor neurons

Hypothesis. In TARDBP-mutant ALS motor neurons, increased CDK5-dependent phosphorylation of NUP98 reduces its residence at nuclear pores, causing nuclear-import failure before persistent cytoplasmic TDP-43 assemblies emerge. Reduced import subsequently promotes nuclear TDP-43 depletion and neuronal dysfunction. Here, “initiating” means initiating the transport defect downstream of the genetic lesion—not initiating every form of ALS. Selecting NUP98 as a nucleoporin candidate and CDK5 as a kinase candidate uses unverified prior knowledge. Their proposed interaction and phosphorylation-dependent effects are assumptions, not packet findings.

Supported premises. Disease-linked TDP-43 can disrupt nucleoporin localization and nuclear transport, and pore pathology occurs in ALS tissue [S1]. Persistent cytoplasmic TDP-43 assemblies can accompany import inhibition, nuclear TDP-43 depletion, and cell death without conventional stress granules [S3]. Stress granules provide another route by recruiting transport factors and impairing transport [S4]. C9orf72 repeat-associated RanGAP mislocalization and import defects establish a distinct genetic-context-specific route, not evidence for the proposed CDK5–NUP98 mechanism [S2]. None of these sources establishes nucleoporin phosphorylation as an initiating lesion; phosphorylated TDP-43 in [S3] is not evidence of phosphorylated NUP98.

Speculative bridges. The proposed chain requires mutant TDP-43-associated signaling to increase CDK5 activity before substantial assembly formation; CDK5 must directly phosphorylate NUP98; and that modification must reduce pore retention rather than merely accompany altered protein abundance. NUP98 displacement must then impair import sufficiently to reduce nuclear TDP-43. Each link requires independent testing. Subsequent TDP-43 assemblies could amplify transport failure without being its initial cause.

Alternatives. Transport-factor sequestration by persistent TDP-43 assemblies or stress granules could occur first, with NUP98 phosphorylation appearing as a downstream stress response [S3, S4]. Alternatively, broader cellular stress could independently produce both phosphorylation and transport failure. Blocking conventional stress granules alone would not distinguish these possibilities because the assembly-associated route in [S3] does not require them.

Discriminating preclinical strategy. Use several TARDBP-mutant patient-derived induced pluripotent stem-cell lines, isogenic corrected controls, and independently differentiated spinal motor neurons. Obtain longitudinal measurements beginning before detectable transport defects. Quantify endogenous NUP98 phosphosite occupancy, total abundance, pore localization, and CDK5 activity. Measure import kinetics with two independently designed import reporters, alongside export and passive-permeability controls. Track nuclear TDP-43, persistent cytoplasmic assemblies, stress granules, cellular stress, and neuronal survival. The predicted order is NUP98 phosphorylation, reduced pore residence, import impairment, and then nuclear TDP-43 depletion and dysfunction. Survival is a secondary endpoint; early import kinetics are the primary endpoint.

Map the candidate sites in a discovery cohort, test direct phosphorylation by CDK5 biochemically, and lock the sites before validation in independent lines. Introduce endogenous phospho-null substitutions at those sites, with precise wild-type revertants. Require normal baseline NUP98 abundance, pore localization, and import in corrected neurons before interpreting protection. Combine this substrate-specific intervention with acute CDK5 suppression and verify actual loss of the relevant phosphorylation. Kinase inhibition alone would be insufficient evidence because other substrates could mediate rescue.

For sufficiency, use inducible proximity-directed recruitment of active CDK5 to NUP98 in corrected neurons, with catalytically inactive and untargeted controls. Confirm phosphorylation at the locked sites and test whether pore displacement and import failure occur before assemblies or generalized stress. Loss of this effect in phospho-null neurons would strengthen substrate attribution. A phosphomimetic allele alone would not establish sufficiency. Separately suppress conventional stress granules and persistent TDP-43 assemblies, preserving TDP-43 abundance and verifying suppression. Persistence of phosphorylation-dependent import failure would favor the intrinsic pore-modification mechanism over sequestration.

Falsification and limitations. The initiating hypothesis is falsified if import failure reproducibly precedes NUP98 phosphorylation, or if functionally intact phospho-null neurons retain the early pore and import defects despite verified elimination of the modification. Rescue by assembly suppression despite persistent NUP98 phosphorylation would also undermine the proposed causal chain. Limited neuronal maturation, undetected small assemblies, structural effects of substitutions, and phosphorylation of neighboring proteins during kinase recruitment constrain interpretation. Even positive results would establish a preclinical mechanism in the tested TARDBP context, not a universal ALS cause or validated treatment.

Ranked proposal:
CDK5-dependent NUP98 phosphorylation initiates nuclear-import failure in TARDBP-mutant motor neurons
